dok_rationale: Part (c) selects a sampling method by linking grade differences in sleep to representation, then explains why randomness does not make the three plans equivalent.
stem: Suppose a school with four grades of 300 students each wants to estimate nightly hours of sleep. Three teams propose samples of 50.\par\smallskip \textbf{Method 1:} Choose a random start among the first 24 names on the alphabetical roster, then take every 24th name.\par \textbf{Method 2:} Put all 1{,}200 names in a hat, mix thoroughly, and draw 50 without replacement.\par \textbf{Method 3:} Separate the roster by grade, then randomly choose 12 students from each grade, then choose two grades at random and add one more randomly chosen student from each, for 50 total.\par\smallskip A student says, \emph{They all use randomness, so they are the same.}
first_take: Would these plans give the school the same mix of students every time? Give one reason from the plans.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name each method: systematic random, simple random, or stratified random.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Which method is an SRS of 50 students? Explain using what must have an equal chance, not just the word random.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suppose sleep differs a lot by grade. Choose a method and explain what it guarantees about the mix of grades. Contrast it with the other two methods, then respond to the student's claim that all three are the same.

answers.a: Method 1 is systematic random sampling. Method 2 is a simple random sample. Method 3 is stratified random sampling, with grade as the stratum.
answers.b: Method 2 is the SRS because every possible group of 50 students has an equal chance to be drawn. Method 1 allows only groups generated by one of 24 starts, and Method 3 forces 12 or 13 students from each grade, so neither gives every group of 50 an equal chance.
answers.c: Choose Method 3: it guarantees 12 or 13 randomly selected students from each grade, so a grade with different sleep habits cannot be left out. Methods 1 and 2 do not fix the number from each grade, even though both use chance. All three can be random without allowing the same possible groups or guaranteeing the same grade mix.

expectedElements.description: Chooses Method 3 because grade is related to sleep
Explains 12 or 13 per grade versus no required grade counts in Methods 1 and 2
Explains that use of chance does not make the possible samples or guarantees identical

scoringGuide.E: All three elements are correct and linked to this problem. Accept equivalent plain-language reasoning.
scoringGuide.P: At least one element includes a correct evidence-to-reason link, but another is missing or incorrect.
scoringGuide.I: No correct evidence-to-reason link; only a choice, copied numbers, or unsupported statements.

commonMistakes: Calling every random method an SRS
Calling sampling within every grade cluster sampling
Claiming an SRS guarantees equal grade counts
